title: The Galvanometer Bench
summary: Turn a galvanometer into an ammeter or voltmeter, and compare how sensitive different coils are.
subject: physics
concepts: Galvanometer to voltmeter, the series resistor
Current and voltage sensitivity of a coil
learningOutcome: The student can find the sensitivity and full-scale current of a galvanometer, design a shunt or series resistor for an ammeter or voltmeter, and compare current and voltage sensitivity.

levels.title: Pointer and spring
levels.adds: Baseline: NIAB = kθ, so the deflection per unit current is NAB/k (Section 4.10).
hints: Slide the current and read the deflection to see the sensitivity.
Calculate NAB/k with A in m² and k in N m/rad, then convert radians to degrees.

levels.title: The ammeter
levels.adds: New idea: a shunt in parallel takes the rest of the current, and the ammeter must have a small resistance (Example 4.12).
hints: At full range the shunt and the coil have the same voltage: I_g R_G = (I − I_g) r_s.
Convert amperes and milliamperes with care, and give r_s in mΩ.
The ammeter has a small resistance of its own, in series with the 3 Ω.

levels.title: The voltmeter
levels.adds: New idea: a large series resistor limits the current drawn, and R + R_G = V/I_g (Section 4.10).
hints: At full range V drives I_g through the coil and the series resistor together.
The voltmeter resistance is the whole of R + R_G.

levels.title: Two meters
levels.adds: More steps: current sensitivity is NAB/k and voltage sensitivity is NAB/kR (Ex 4.10).
hints: The springs are the same, so the ratio of the current sensitivities is the ratio of NAB.
Voltage sensitivity has the coil resistance R in the denominator as well.
Take the ratio of each quantity, meter 2 over meter 1.

levels.title: More turns
levels.adds: Misconception check: more turns raise the current sensitivity but leave the voltage sensitivity unchanged (Section 4.10).
hints: The current sensitivity NAB/k is proportional to N.
The resistance of the coil is also proportional to N.
So NAB/kR does not change with N.

misconceptions: A galvanometer can measure large currents directly
A shunt is connected in series with the galvanometer
A voltmeter should have a small resistance
More turns always make a more sensitive voltmeter
